doc.title: Darius Brubeck interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 29, 2024

title: Cultural boycott, the UDF and welcoming visiting artists
summary: On the boycott, the UDF, Johnny Clegg's SAMA, Sun City, and how artists who supported the struggle gave workshops at Natal.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Did you agree with the Artists United Against Apartheid? Did you feel that that refusal to come in ensuing years was a positive or a negative?

Well the UDF, the United Democratic Front, which was an open organization, it wasn’t a banned organization like the ANC, the African National Congress. The United Democratic Front always kind of apologetically said to the South African public that a boycott is a blunt instrument and you know we can’t always choose between the good guys and the bad guys, so you know we’ll just say a boycott’s a boycott. But then there were so many individual exceptions that refined — made the blunt instrument rather surgical. But as I recall, now we’re talking about between 40 and 30 years ago so my memory may not be totally adequate on this because — that’s not in the book — but UDF was primarily driven by or let’s say staffed by — because it was driven by genuine popular movement but it was staffed by people who had the leisure and the education and an office were people in the labor union movement and they were the people that we actually talked to. And the people that they talked to overseas were correspondingly affiliated with labor unions in different countries, in the United Kingdom, France and the Netherlands, Germany. So there were always channels of communication. And then, and this is in the book, finally — this part, not the part I just told you — Johnny Clegg — do you know who Johnny Clegg was? You know quite a cultural hero and a unique individual on many levels, got together the South African — SAMA — South African Music Association. So then we had like an official channel then, because it had a proven popular base and musicians joined it or not. They were free not to but those who already had international careers certainly found it to their advantage. And that became a way of negotiating all these political difficulties. And the usual agreement was that we would be very disapproving of artists who simply came to play in Sun City, which very often would be the anchor date for big names and we didn’t even recognize that Bophuthatswana was really a country, although that was again a kind of boycott busting
maneuver to say well it’s an independent country. You know a casino state. There were several such.

So called tribal homelands that in effect were funded by gambling. And so we’d be down on that but then on the other hand like you know when artists came who identified with the struggle, and you could tell that pretty easily by the content of their music, their shows, the make-up of their band, they were welcomed, usually on the condition that they provided some kind of outreach, you know usually in the form of a workshop or workshops from members of the group, and then people on the other end — well by then I was in charge of the jazz program at the University of Natal as it then was, so I would host some major people on campus and students would benefit from contact with them. And that was all fine. There was no political damage to their careers when they did what we perceived to be the right thing.
